analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every legal resident health coverage through state programs funded by new payroll and income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors: referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in May 1993, it never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a universal health coverage program: every legal resident would be enrolled automatically in their state's program and issued a MediCORE card covering medically necessary care, prescription drugs, mental health, preventive services, long-term care, and a cap on out-of-pocket catastrophic costs. States would run the programs under a new Federal MediCORE Board in the Department of Health and Human Services, and the bill would fold Medicare, Medicaid, and CHAMPUS financing into a single trust fund. The money would come from new taxes: 2 percent on employee wages, 4 percent on employers with no wage cap, a progressive tax on higher incomes up to 6 percent, and the elimination of the tax breaks that sustain employer-based private insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Every legal resident, especially the roughly 37 million uninsured Americans of that era and families wiped out by medical bills. Coverage would be automatic and portable from birth, preventive care would carry no cost sharing, total cost sharing could not exceed 15 percent of covered costs, and catastrophic expenses would be capped. People would no longer lose coverage when changing or losing jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and families facing medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Makes every legal resident of the United States, including lawful resident aliens, eligible for a defined package of CORE services, with automatic enrollment at birth and default enrollment for anyone else.

Requires the covered package to include medically necessary services such as prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive services with no cost sharing, long-term care options, and a cap on what an individual owes for catastrophic care.
Caps total premiums, copayments, and deductibles at 15 percent of covered costs, and bars any cost sharing on preventive care.

Replaces the employer-based insurance system, which the bill's findings describe as leaving the poor and elderly uncovered and driving family health costs up 147 percent in the 1980s, and supersedes ERISA so coverage follows the person rather than the job.

analysis.who_pays: Working people and employers, through new taxes: 2 percent of wages from employees, 4 percent from employers with no cap on the employer-side wages taxed, up to 6 percent of adjusted gross income from individuals above small thresholds, plus the loss of employer health plan tax exclusions. Health insurers lose the employer-based market, since private insurance could only be sold for services the program does not cover.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers through new payroll taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on nearly everyone who works: a 2 percent employee payroll tax, a 4 percent employer payroll tax with no wage cap, and a progressive individual tax reaching 6 percent of adjusted gross income, while simultaneously ending the tax exclusion for employer health contributions.

The scope of benefits is left to the discretion of a nine-member board appointed by the President, which must reconcile the covered services against whatever the trust fund can afford, so the actual benefit package would depend on the financing available.

States whose programs fail the federal board's approval could be placed in receivership and run directly by the board, and providers are treated as having agreed to accept the state reimbursement as payment in full, limiting their pricing and billing freedom.
The MediCORE trust fund and its taxes are placed off-budget, exempt from general budget limits, which weakens fiscal oversight of what would be one of the largest programs in government.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a single-payer-style universal coverage plan with a genuine cost-containment design: it pooled everyone, paid providers fixed rates, capped cost sharing, and funded itself with broad-based taxes while ending the tax break that props up employer insurance. The gains for the uninsured and the medically bankrupt would have been enormous, and the bill's own findings argue existing spending was sufficient to pay for coverage. The costs are real and broadly distributed, however, since nearly every worker and employer would pay new taxes, the benefit package would rest on unelected board discretion and available funds, and the off-budget trust fund complicates accountability. It never got a hearing, so none of this was ever tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote there, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the MediCORE Health Act of 1993 on May 27, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No senator joined as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the referral.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers were better off: employers avoided a new 4 percent uncapped payroll tax while keeping their insurance tax breaks, and insurers kept the employer-based market the bill would have eliminated. Americans without coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and health insurers, not the uninsured

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: 1993-94 health care reform opponents
against.role: Insurers, employers, and allied groups active during the 1993-94 health reform debate
against.what_they_did: Ran a national campaign against government-structured universal health coverage during the same Congress, in which every comprehensive bill failed without reaching a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan divide never showed up in the record; the lone sponsor was a Republican, while the committee that shelved it was run by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would end employer-based private insurance, the industry's core market, by taxing employer health contributions and allowing private coverage only for services the public program does not cover. Its death preserved the existing insurance market.

Employers would owe a new 4 percent payroll tax with no wage cap but would shed their employee health insurance obligations and lose the tax exclusion for them. Stopping the bill preserved the status quo of employer-managed coverage.

industries.industry: Managed care organizations and claims administrators
industries.note: States would be encouraged to run competing delivery plans and could contract with private carriers and managed care organizations to administer the program, making these firms the permanent administrative and delivery channel for universal coverage.

Providers would gain a paying patient pool covering every resident, but must accept state-set rates as payment in full, bar balance billing, and operate under board-guided malpractice reform including damage caps.
